c0006: Average number of events you serve per year, counting every corporate booking, wedding, private party and festival or farmers market day. It is the main volume driver of the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, and years 2 and 3 grow in events. The example is a full-time owner-operator with an active corporate sales effort and two stations, not the average first year. Flashquotes shows about 15 bookings per operator per year on its own platform only, so do not read that as the events to expect. Compare this cell with the capacity row further down.
c0008: EXCL. sales tax, with the baristas, travel and extras included and the voluntary gratuity left out: the blended price per guest across everything you sell (hosted corporate and wedding bookings, private parties, festival days), not the price of any one package. Price per guest incl. sales tax = this value × (1 + your sales tax rate). Operators quote by booking and by hour, with a base fee plus an hourly rate (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). The Pricing Calculator quotes per guest, per service hour and per drink: to bring a quote here, divide the revenue you bill in a year by the guests you serve in that year.
c0010: Average number of guests per event across your whole mix, from small private parties to weddings of well over a hundred guests. The typical Flashquotes booking is for 100 guests. At a festival or farmers market, every drink sold counts as one guest. Sales per event = guests × price per guest. One cell for the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, so they always agree.
c0012: Growth in events in year 2 over year 1 (enter 0.10 for 10%). Kept conservative on purpose: repeat corporate clients build up slowly, wedding bookings are made months ahead, and two stations and a small team of baristas limit how fast you can grow.
c0014: Growth in events in year 3 over year 2, kept conservative for the same reason: corporate repeat business and planner referrals build up slowly, and two stations and your baristas limit how many events you can serve.
c0018: Share of sales that comes from coffee bar packages: the espresso bar with baristas, batch brew and cold brew, milks, syrups and compostable cups. It is an INPUT: change it here and the P&L, the cash flow and the sales tax collected recalculate on their own. The rest of your sales are add-ons.
c0020: Calculated as the remainder: coffee bar packages + add-ons = 100%. Add-ons are extra service hours, branded cups and latte printing, pastries from a licensed bakery and travel fees.
c0022: Cost of goods sold on coffee bar package sales: coffee (18 g, or 0.63 oz, per double), milk and oat milk, syrups and cold brew, with a 10% allowance for waste (purging, dialing in, leftover milk). Kit estimate built from an all-in cost of $0.75-1.50 per drink (grindkit.app). The cost of one drink from the calculator is not copied here: this cell is the average of your whole mix, and package revenue also pays for the baristas, so the share is lower than the 20-30% that GrindKit reports on drink revenue. It is the most sensitive lever in the plan: test it at the top of the range before you trust the result.
c0024: Cost of goods sold on add-ons: pastries bought from a licensed bakery, branded cups and printing ink. Extra hours and travel fees carry almost no cost of goods. Kit estimate.
c0026: Compostable cups, lids, sleeves, wooden stirrers and napkins as a % of sales (about $0.30 per drink: Kit estimate). They are compostable because several cities require it (Seattle, as an example): check your local rules. The line scales with the number of drinks you serve. Fuel is NOT here: tow vehicle fuel has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab, and generator fuel is in utilities.
c0028: Share of your sales that comes from festivals and farmers markets where each guest pays for their own drink, often with a minimum sales guarantee from the organizer. This is a side channel, not a delivery or marketplace channel. Set it to 0 if you only work hosted events. The organizer keeps a fee (next row).
c0030: Fee the organizer keeps on your festival and farmers market sales (Kit estimate). If you pay a flat booth fee instead, convert it into a percentage of what you expect to sell there. Not used while the festival share is 0%.
c0032: Card and ACH fees on total sales. Hosts pay their retainer and balance by card, festival guests almost always pay by card, and some companies pay by ACH or check, which lowers the cost. The example is a blended rate: a percentage plus a per-transaction fee, which weighs more on small orders. Check your processor's statement and enter your effective rate (Kit estimate).
c0042: Monthly cost of your commissary (a permitted shared kitchen), cart storage and trailer parking: one cell for everything you pay for the space. It covers filling potable water, dumping gray water, cold storage for the milk, dry storage and a place for the cart and the trailer. Carts typically pay $200-600 per month (cart-king.com) and shared kitchens charge roughly $15-45 per hour (The Food Corridor, 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey). The deposit and the months before opening are calculated from it. Ask your health department in writing whether your county requires a commissary: many do, and some exempt self-contained units. Get quotes in your area before you sign.
c0044: Months of deposit on the commissary agreement. Many shared kitchens ask for one month up front: far less than the deposit on a commercial lease. Negotiate it in the written agreement.
c0046: Generator fuel, water and ice that the commissary fee does not cover. The generator only runs at outdoor events, because most venues provide power, so this is a small fixed amount. Tow vehicle fuel is not here: it has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab. It is the one cell for this cost, so you change it in one place and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0048: General liability at $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate with unlimited additional insureds, commercial auto that covers the trailer, workers' comp for your W-2 baristas and coverage for your equipment in transit. Venues ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured. There is no liquor liability line because this plan sells no alcohol. Insureon publishes averages for small businesses (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab); the example is a Kit estimate, so get quotes from an insurance agent. It is counted once, as an annual expense, not also in startup costs.
c0050: Extra milk, ice, cables and parking at the venue: the unbudgeted costs of each event. It is a VARIABLE cost: it rises and falls with the number of events, so it cannot sit among the fixed costs or it would move the break-even without anyone noticing. Tow vehicle fuel is not here: it has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab.
c0053: Your own money. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%) on the total cash needed in this plan.
c0055: Principal requested: bank or SBA 7(a). The example loan is above the $50,000 ceiling of the SBA Microloan, so it fits an SBA 7(a) loan or a bank loan (or a Microloan with more of your own money). If your loan is an SBA 7(a), this is the cell. It is the only loan that the amortization schedule, the P&L interest and the DSCR use. The "Financing" tab checks that the sources of funds match the total cash needed on the "Startup Costs" tab (which includes working capital and the cart, portable bar, trailer and plan review contingency): copy the loan suggested there into this cell until the difference reaches zero. A lender will ask for your plan and projections.
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example (10%) is the kit's assumption for an SBA 7(a) loan. A smaller loan secured by a cart, a trailer and espresso equipment often prices above a storefront loan: ask two lenders for quotes, and ask about SBA-guaranteed loans, before you set it.
c0059: Total years, interest-only period included. A cart, a portable bar, a trailer and espresso machines lose value faster than a storefront build-out, so the term is shorter. SBA 7(a) allows up to 10 years for equipment and working capital.
c0079: The espresso cart, the portable espresso bar, the enclosed trailer with its wrap and fit-out, and the plan review: the assets that travel to the event are depreciated together. Straight-line book depreciation; tax methods such as MACRS or Section 179 are separate, so confirm with your accountant.
c0081: Espresso machines, grinders, generator and cords, batch brewer and cold brew system, smallwares, POS and software. Loading and unloading at every event wears them faster than a fixed bar, so a short life is prudent; burrs and gaskets are replaced sooner and go in maintenance. Straight-line book depreciation; MACRS or Section 179 are tax treatments: confirm with your accountant.
c0087: INFORMATION ONLY: it does not enter any calculation in this workbook. It is your estimate of the most events a year your two stations and your baristas can handle. Weekdays have room because corporate events fill them; Saturdays in the wedding season are the bottleneck. Compare it with the events per year you plan and with the optimistic scenario: if the plan goes above it, you need a third station or more baristas. Volume itself is driven by the "Events per year" cell above.
c0089: A new coffee catering company does not book in month one what it books in month eight: corporate clients want to try you first, and the median booking is made about 41 days ahead (Flashquotes), with weddings earlier. Events per year above is the year-1 AVERAGE: the ramp only spreads year 1's sales across the months (slower start, stronger finish) and keeps the annual total. At 100% there is no ramp. Festivals and farmers markets are an add-on channel, never a daily street route (that is the Food Truck Kit).
c0093: Getting the commissary agreement, the plan review and the cart inspection done takes weeks, and you test both stations and hold a corporate open house before your first booking, so you pay commissary rent before you earn anything. It belongs in startup costs, not in the P&L.
c0095: Calculated by formula on the espresso cart, portable bar, trailer, trailer wrap and plan review lines: if you change the cart price, the contingency recalculates on its own. The note on that row of the "Startup Costs" tab lists exactly which lines are included.
c0098: Average days between the event and the money in your bank. Hosts usually pay a retainer of 30-50% when they book the date (grindkit.app) and the balance 14 days before the event, while companies often pay at 15-30 days, so the example sits in between. Raise it if your clients pay later. The workbook does not model deposits: they improve your real cash flow.
c0106: ZERO by default: a coffee cart sells no alcohol. Espresso martinis belong to a licensed mobile bar (see the Mobile Bar Business Plan Kit). Selling alcohol requires a liquor license (and, in some states, an event-by-event permit): check your state before adding it. If you ever add it, carry liquor liability coverage.
c0108: Only used if you enter alcohol sales above, which is zero in this plan. Example rate: the same as the rest of the sales (state + local combined). Some states tax alcohol at a different rate or add liquor taxes: if you sell alcohol, enter the rate that applies.
c0144: Espresso cart with NSF certification, handwashing sink, potable and gray water tanks (your county sets the volume), pump and filter, and an under-counter refrigerator. Prices run from a few thousand dollars for a basic new cart to well above that for a custom build (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). Ask your county for its plan review checklist BEFORE you buy the cart.
c0147: Portable espresso bar for the second station and for indoor rooms, with an under-counter refrigerator (Kit estimate). It travels in the trailer with the cart.
c0149: A 2-group volumetric machine at 220V / 3,400 W (about $8,500-9,000 in store prices; NEMA 6-20 plug, 15-17 A, dedicated circuit) plus a compact 2-group machine for the second station (about $7,200, 14 A). Store prices are a Kit estimate: ask for two quotes. A room without a 220V circuit needs a generator.
c0151: Four espresso grinders (house blend and decaf at each station), $300-3,000 each (cart-king.com). Burrs wear out sooner than the grinder: they go in the maintenance line of the "3-Year P&L" tab.
c0153: An enclosed cargo trailer, 6×12 ft with a ramp door, that carries the cart, the portable bar and the gear. Your own vehicle tows it ($0 in the example). If you do not have a tow vehicle, a used one runs about $18,000 and is not in the budget.
c0155: Trailer wrap, hitch, tie-downs on E-track and ramps to roll the cart in and out. Check your vehicle's towing capacity and that your insurance covers the wrap and the hitch.
c0157: State filing fees for the LLC (Secretary of State) plus an attorney's review of your standard contract (retainer, cancellation tiers, final guest count, service hours, outlet or generator, rain plan) or a filing service; a registered agent is also needed. Fees vary a lot by state. The "Taxable / recoverable tax?" column is set to No: it only matters if you enter a recoverable input tax rate (for example UK VAT).
c0160: Varies a lot by city, county and state: get the amounts for yours before you close the budget. Expect the health permit for the mobile food unit, food handler cards, a Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) certificate, the business license, the sales tax permit and, where required, a fire marshal permit for the generator.
c0162: Plan review of the mobile food unit and inspection of the cart. As an example, Snohomish County, WA charges $1,100 for the plan review (snohd.org); add any electrical approval your state asks for. Rules and fees vary by county, so ask the health department for its fee schedule. If nobody charges for it, enter 0.
c0164: POS with card readers (also for festivals), plus booking software for quotes, proposals and e-signatures.
c0166: Batch brewer, airpots, a cold brew system, milk pitchers, scales, tampers, knock boxes, sanitizer buckets and storage racks for the commissary: the tools that get depreciated. Daily disposables are NOT depreciated: they go in the compostable cups line of the P&L, at the % of sales set in the "0. Assumptions" tab.
c0168: Coffee for your tastings and first events, milks, syrups and compostable cups. With 0% recoverable input tax (the US default), any sales tax you pay on this purchase is treated as a cost.
c0170: Website, photos from real events, tastings, a corporate open house and your first bridal show, plus listings on The Knot, Zola and GigSalad.
c0172: A 5,500 W continuous inverter generator (quiet, for rooms without an outlet and for outdoor events), cords of the right gauge and a power strip with GFCI. Your fire marshal may ask for a minimum distance and a fire extinguisher: ask before you buy.
c0180: What you buy: the cart and the portable bar, the espresso machines and grinders, the trailer, power, launch and formation costs. The cash cushion is not an investment: it is working capital.
c0205: Sales of coffee bar packages: the espresso bar with baristas, batch brew and cold brew, milks, syrups and compostable cups, across corporate events, weddings, private parties and festival days. All of it carries cost of goods sold at the package rate.
c0207: Sales of add-ons: extra hours, branded cups and latte printing, pastries from a licensed bakery and travel fees. There is no alcohol revenue.
c0213: Applied to the sales of THAT CHANNEL. With 0% festival and farmers market sales in "0. Assumptions", this line is zero
c0221: The monthly amount is typed in "0. Assumptions"; here it is multiplied by twelve. It covers your commissary hours, cart storage and trailer parking, not storefront rent. The months before opening are on the "Startup Costs" tab and are NOT counted twice.
c0225: Generator fuel, water and ice that the commissary fee does not cover. Tow vehicle fuel is not here: it has its own fixed line on this tab.
c0235: Phone, internet and the data plans of your card readers and POS. Small, fixed and easy to forget.
c0237: Service for the espresso machines, water filters and grinder burrs. Gaskets and burrs wear out before the machine does.
c0239: Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) and food handler cards for you and your team, plus their renewals, and barista training. The required cards vary by state.
c0241: Food cost and labor for the tastings you offer couples and companies (a bridal tasting or a corporate open house). Many operators charge a fee and credit it toward the booking: if you do, lower this line.
c0265: Floor set by this workbook: kit benchmark (editable estimate). The workbook's gross margin also subtracts compostable cups, card fees, festival organizer fees and miscellaneous costs, so the floor sits below the margin you would see on cost of goods alone.
c0268: Ceiling for cost of goods (compostable cups have their own line): kit benchmark (editable estimate), based on the 20-30% cost of goods that GrindKit reports for drink revenue.
c0270: Ceiling: kit benchmark (editable estimate), set above what many pricing guides report because it includes the owner's own pay as lead barista and sales.
c0272: There is no storefront rent in this workbook: 6% is a prudent ceiling for the commissary, cart storage and trailer parking, a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A business with its own fixed location carries a much higher occupancy cost.
c0274: Floor of 5%: a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A new business with a loan to repay starts lower than established operators.
c0324: The SAME staffing in all three scenarios. In the pessimistic case your real event-staff cost falls with the number of events (you pay hours per event), so the real result would be somewhat better than shown. If labor cost still blows up, adjust it in the "Staffing" tab, not here
c0344: Sells to companies and couples, runs the tastings and works the espresso bar at the events. Covers the main shift at every event. The rest of the owner's pay comes from profit.
c0346: Lead barista, part-time W-2: runs the second station and the second event of the day. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE, around the 90th percentile of occupation 35-3023 (BLS OEWS, May 2025: $20.51 per hour) because event baristas earn more ($20-35 per hour at grindkit.app).
c0348: Event baristas hired per event and paid hourly as W-2 employees, with one barista for every 50-65 drinks an hour (Flashquotes). Their FTE is a fraction because they only work event hours. Treating them as 1099 contractors is a misclassification risk (FLSA; California AB5). Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE. Voluntary tips are theirs.
c0350: On-call barista and driver, hourly W-2: reinforces the team in March-May and December, loads the trailer and tows it to the venue. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0364: Hours of work per person for one event: loading at the commissary, travel, about one hour of setup, 2-2.5 hours of service, and breakdown and cleanup. A 2-hour event takes 7-9 hours of shift (grindkit.app). Serving is only part of it. Hours × people × events per year sets the event staff cost.
c0366: Average number of baristas working each event: 1 at small parties and quiet festivals, 2 at weddings and large company events (Kit estimate from 50-65 drinks per barista per hour). Weighted by the mix in the Word plan, the average is about 1.6. Raise it if you staff more heavily: the staffing sizes itself.
c0379: 1. "0. Assumptions" is the control sheet: events per year, price per guest excl. sales tax, guests per event, the mix of coffee bar packages and add-ons, cost of goods sold, commissary and cart storage, financing and taxes.
c0386: 8. The Word business plan in this kit uses the same example figures as this workbook. The workbook is the one that recalculates on its own when you change a green cell: if you change one, update the matching figures in the Word document.
c0419: Commissary, cart storage and trailer parking
c0420: Left out: the model shows no cost of space
c0421: A monthly cost for the commissary, cart storage and trailer parking, plus a deposit and rent for the months before opening
c0422: The coffee is brewed at the event, but the water, the milk and the cart need a permitted commissary to start from and come back to. Leaving it out makes the business look like it has no occupancy cost.
c0428: One useful life for everything, including items that are not fixed assets
c0429: Two useful lives: the cart, portable bar, trailer and their fit-out on one, and the espresso machines, grinders, generator and other equipment on the other. The Startup Costs tab calculates the annual charge.
c0430: The cart, bar and trailer wear out at a different speed than the machines, grinders and generator. Working capital, opening inventory and launch marketing are not fixed assets, so they are not depreciated.
c0431: Trailer and equipment insurance, and liability
c0432: Counted twice: once in startup costs and again as an annual expense
c0433: Counted once, as an annual expense
c0434: Counting a premium in both places inflates the startup costs, the cash you need to raise and the loan you ask for.
c0436: A separate fuel line, on top of utilities
c0437: Included in the utilities line, in one monthly cell
c0438: Generator fuel, water and ice rise and fall with how many events are outdoors: here they live in one cell, and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0440: A lump sum typed by hand
c0441: A percentage calculated on the cart, portable bar, trailer, wrap and plan review lines
c0442: If you change the cart price, the contingency recalculates instead of staying at the old amount.
c0460: A miscellaneous line typed in among the fixed costs
c0461: A percentage of sales, treated as a variable cost; tow vehicle fuel has its own fixed line
c0462: Extra milk, ice, cables and venue parking rise and fall with the number of events: among the fixed costs they would distort the break-even.
c0463: Cost of goods on all sales
c0464: Revenue with no cost of goods sold attached
c0465: Every sale carries its cost of goods: coffee bar packages and add-ons each at their own rate
c0466: A revenue line that pays for no ingredients shows a margin that does not exist.
c0479: Typical event: 100 guests. P10 $612, P90 $3,000. Based on 25,860 bookings from 578 operators (April 2023 to April 2026). Your price depends on hours, guests and market.
c0480: Price per guest by event size
c0481: Under 50 guests about $38; 50-99 about $18; 100-249 about $13; 250-499 about $11
c0483: GrindKit calls $5-11 per guest at 100 guests healthy and anything under $5 a loss. Price per guest drops as events get bigger.
c0485: Up to 2 hours 1.0; 2-4 hours 1.3-1.5; 4-6 hours 1.5-1.8; 6+ hours 2.0-2.5
c0487: Add 20-30% for morning events. At a festival, count each drink sold as one guest.
c0489: Plan review $1,100; annual permit $500, $745 or $1,025 by risk level
c0491: Snohomish County, WA, as an example: electrical approval comes first. Fees and rules differ by county, so ask yours before you buy a cart.
c0493: 1 cart with 1 barista 50-65; 2 carts with 2 baristas about 100
c0495: Flashquotes suggests 2-3 baristas for about 250 guests, and Coffee Cart Boys cites 50 cups per hour. The "Staffing" tab uses this pace to size your crew.
c0499: Double shot $0.25-0.45, milk $0.20-0.40, oat milk $0.60-1.10, cup and lid $0.20-0.45. Cost of goods runs 20-30% of drink revenue.
c0500: Startup cost of a coffee cart
c0501: $5,000-25,000 for a cart; a 2-group machine about $8,500
c0503: Cart-king.com lists a typical cart at $24,000 and a premium one at $49,000. The $5,000-25,000 range and the machine price (store price) are Kit estimates.
c0505: Ground coffee $9.33 per lb; whole milk $4.11 per gal
c0507: National averages for September 2026 (series APU0000717311 and APU0000709112). Wholesale specialty coffee runs about $18 per lb (Kit estimate).
c0509: Base fee $300-500 plus $150-200 per service hour; travel fee $1.25 per mile round trip
c0511: Operators ask for a retainer of 30-50% to hold the date and the balance 14 days before the event. The kit's contract applies the retainer to the price.
c0515: BLS has no occupation of its own for baristas: they sit inside 35-3023, Fast Food and Counter Workers. Event baristas earn more, $20-35 per hour at grindkit.app.
c0519: 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey; 42% of operators charge $20-$29 per hour. A cart pays mostly for storage and water access, $200-600 per month (cart-king.com), and not every kitchen lets you park a trailer on site.
c0523: Share of coffee cart bookings by month on Flashquotes. For coffee carts, July books about a third of December: plan your cash for the summer dip.
c0527: Insureon averages for businesses under 5 employees: general liability, BOP, workers' comp and commercial auto. Your quotes will differ. Venues usually ask for unlimited additional insureds, and your commercial auto must cover the trailer.
c0529: 20-30% of quotes become bookings; median 41 days' notice
c0531: A close rate above 30% suggests your prices are too low. The 41-day median is why the launch ramp in "0. Assumptions" starts slowly.
c0597: The same calculation on what you BUY (the cart and the portable bar, machines and grinders, trailer, power, launch and formation costs), without working capital: that money is not spent, it is tied up and comes back when the business closes. For reference only: the payback that matters is the one above
